name: Mona Lisa
info: The Mona Lisa is a half-length oil portrait on a poplar panel by Leonardo da Vinci, traditionally held to show Lisa del Giocondo, begun in Florence around 1503 and kept in the Louvre in Paris since 1797.

facts.made: Leonardo da Vinci, probably for the Florentine silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo and his wife Lisa, though some scholars name a different commission; Leonardo never gave it to the Giocondo family
facts.form: A half-length portrait in oil on a white poplar panel, showing a seated woman in three-quarter profile before a landscape, painted without outlines in the soft blending called sfumato
facts.where: The Louvre, Paris, where it has normally been on display since 1797, in a climate-controlled enclosure behind bulletproof glass in the Salle des États
facts.known: the sitter's ambiguous expression; sfumato modelling; an imaginary landscape behind the figure; Leonardo's long work on it; the theft of 1911; its influence on later portraits and on avant-garde parody

t: Leonardo was working on a portrait of Lisa del Giocondo by October 1503, but he never gave the painting to her family, and he may have continued to work on it as late as 1517.
The portrait was one of the first Italian portraits to set the sitter before an imaginary landscape, and Raphael borrowed from its composition within a few years.
It passed to Francis I of France, hung in the Louvre from 1797 and became widely known partly through its theft in 1911 by Vincenzo Peruggia, who believed it should belong to Italy.
dyk: A marginal note of October 1503 in a 1477 printing of Cicero, found in 2005 by a scholar at Heidelberg University, likens Leonardo to the Greek painter Apelles and says he was then working on a portrait of Lisa del Giocondo.
ev: A note by Agostino Vespucci records that Leonardo was working on a portrait of Lisa del Giocondo
King Francis I of France acquired the painting after Leonardo's death
The painting went on permanent display at the Louvre
Jean-Marie Hooghstoel carried out the first and most extensive recorded cleaning and revarnishing
Vincenzo Peruggia, a Louvre employee, stole the painting
The painting, recovered after Peruggia tried to sell it in Florence, returned to the Louvre
A rock thrown by Ugo Ungaza Villegas shattered the glass case and dislodged a speck of pigment near the left elbow
After conservation and study, the painting was moved to a purpose-built enclosure in the Salle des États

sections.origins:
The Mona Lisa is a half-length portrait painted in oil on a white poplar panel. It has traditionally been considered to depict Lisa del Giocondo, a member of the Gherardini family of Florence and Tuscany and the wife of the wealthy Florentine silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo. The painting is thought to have been commissioned for the couple's new home and to celebrate the birth of their second son, Andrea. Giorgio Vasari wrote in his biography of Leonardo, published in 1550, 31 years after the artist's death, that Leonardo undertook to paint the portrait of Mona Lisa, the wife of Francesco del Giocondo. Monna is a polite Italian form of address that began as ma donna.

In 2005 a scholar at Heidelberg University found a note dated October 1503, written in the margin of a 1477 printing of a volume by Cicero by Leonardo's contemporary Agostino Vespucci, stating that Leonardo was then working on a painting of Lisa del Giocondo. The Louvre's Vincent Delieuvin said that this was certain, but that it could not be said with absolute certainty that the portrait was the painting in the Louvre. At his death in 1524 Leonardo's assistant Salaì owned a portrait named la Gioconda in his papers, which Leonardo had bequeathed to him.
sections.content:
The woman sits markedly upright in a pozzetto armchair with her arms folded, a sign of a reserved posture, and her gaze is fixed on the observer. The painting bears a strong resemblance to many Renaissance depictions of the Virgin Mary, who was then seen as an ideal for womanhood. She appears alive to an unusual extent, which Leonardo achieved by not drawing outlines. The soft blending called sfumato creates an ambiguous mood, mainly in the corners of the mouth and the corners of the eyes. The sitter has no clearly visible eyebrows or eyelashes, although Vasari describes the eyebrows in detail.

She is shown in three-quarter profile in what appears to be an open loggia, with dark pillar bases on either side. Behind her a vast landscape recedes to icy mountains, winding paths and a distant bridge, giving only the slightest indications of human presence. Leonardo placed the horizon line on a level with the eyes, not at the neck as in his portrait of Ginevra de' Benci, which links the figure with the landscape. The painting was one of the first Italian portraits to show the sitter before an imaginary landscape, although some scholars favour a realistic description, and Leonardo was one of the first painters to use aerial perspective.
sections.making:
The Louvre states that the painting was doubtless painted between 1503 and 1506, and some believe it was begun in 1503 or 1504 in Florence. Martin Kemp says that there are difficulties in confirming the dates with certainty. Alessandro Vezzosi believes the painting is characteristic of Leonardo's style after 1513, and other academics argue from the documents that he painted it from 1513. According to Vasari, Leonardo lingered over it four years and left it unfinished. In 1516 King Francis I invited Leonardo to work at the Clos Lucé near the Château d'Amboise; it is believed that he took the painting with him. Carmen C. Bambach concluded that he probably continued refining it until 1516 or 1517, and his right hand was paralytic around 1517.

A record of an October 1517 visit by Louis d'Aragon says the painting was made for the deceased Giuliano de' Medici, which was likely an error. Because a sketch by Raphael of about 1505 shows the flanking columns more clearly, a number of experts have argued that Leonardo made two versions, while others believe there was only one. In 2007 Pascal Cotte announced that his scans showed the figure originally had eyelashes and eyebrows and that the painting had been reworked several times; in 2020 he alleged an underdrawing transferred by the spolvero technique.
sections.reception:
Early critics such as Vasari in the 16th century and André Félibien in the 17th praised the picture for its realism. By the mid-19th century writers began to regard it as imbued with mystery and romance. In 1859 Théophile Gautier called the sitter a "sphinx of beauty who smiles so mysteriously", and in 1869 Walter Pater described her as "older than the rocks among which she sits". In the 1860s part of the French intelligentsia began to hail it as a masterwork of Renaissance painting, although it was not widely known outside the art world. The Baedeker guide of 1878 called it "the most celebrated work of Leonardo in the Louvre".

By the early 20th century some critics felt that the painting had become a repository for subjective theories. When it was stolen in 1911, Bernard Berenson admitted that it had "simply become an incubus, and [he] was glad to be rid of her." Avant-garde artists made note of its popularity: Dadaists and Surrealists often produced modifications and caricatures. In 1919 Marcel Duchamp created L.H.O.O.Q. by adding a moustache and goatee to a cheap reproduction, and Salvador Dalí painted Self portrait as Mona Lisa in 1954. Andy Warhol made serigraph prints of multiple Mona Lisas after its visit to the United States in 1963.
sections.survival:
Francis I acquired the painting after Leonardo's death in 1519. It was kept at Fontainebleau until Louis XIV moved it to Versailles, where it remained until the French Revolution, and in 1797 it went on permanent display at the Louvre. It was moved to the Brest Arsenal during the Franco-Prussian War and, from 28 August 1939, to a series of châteaux and abbeys and finally the Musée Ingres in Montauban, avoiding the paintings looted by Nazi Germany. On 21 August 1911 Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian patriot who had helped build its glass case, stole it from the Louvre. After two years he tried to sell it to the director of the Uffizi; it was shown at the Uffizi and returned to the Louvre on 4 January 1914. Peruggia served six months in prison and was hailed for his patriotism in Italy.

The panel warped and cracked, and two walnut braces were inserted in the mid-18th to early 19th century. The 1809 cleaning removed some of the uppermost paint layer, leaving a washed-out appearance to the face. A flexible oak frame was fitted in 1951, and in 2004 to 2005 a conservation team replaced the maple crosspieces with sycamore ones. The painting has never been fully restored. After a rock broke its case in 1956, bulletproof glass was used to shield it.
sections.legacy:
The Mona Lisa began influencing Florentine painting even before it was complete. Raphael, who had visited Leonardo's workshop several times, used elements of its composition and format in works such as Young Woman with Unicorn and Portrait of Maddalena Doni, both of about 1506, and borrowed from it again in La velata and the Portrait of Baldassare Castiglione. Frank Zöllner states that none of Leonardo's works exerted more influence on the genre of portraiture, and that it became the definitive example of the Renaissance portrait, seen perhaps not only as the likeness of a real person but as the embodiment of an ideal.

Its fame grew from the mid-19th century and grew far more after the theft of 1911, which was reported worldwide and led to a massive increase in public recognition. During the 20th century it became an object of mass reproduction, merchandising and lampooning. In psychology, the impression that a photographed subject who looks into the lens is looking at every viewer is called the Mona Lisa illusion. Other versions exist: the Prado's, restored in 2012, is now thought to be by a pupil in Leonardo's studio, and the attribution of the Isleworth Mona Lisa to Leonardo is disputed among experts.

summary: The Mona Lisa is Leonardo da Vinci's half-length oil portrait, traditionally held to show Lisa del Giocondo and begun around 1503. Leonardo may have worked on it until 1517. Francis I acquired it, it went to the Louvre in 1797, and its theft in 1911 added greatly to its fame.
references: Roy McMullen, Mona Lisa: The Picture and the Myth (Houghton Mifflin Company, 1975)
Donald Sassoon, Becoming Mona Lisa: The Making of a Global Icon (Harcourt, Inc., 2001)
notes: The article's Further reading lists only two books, so only two references are given.
Dating: the article gives 1503-1506 (the Louvre), 1503 or 1504 (some), post-1513 (Vezzosi and others) and continued work to 1516 or 1517 (Bambach); start 1503 with circa true.
Under the two-version theory the article gives different fates for the paintings (Salaì's possession, a sale to Francis I in 1518); left out, since experts are divided.
Left out: tourism and visitor numbers, insurance valuation, cultural depictions in films, songs and games, and the Cotte hidden-portrait claim beyond the eyelash and reworking findings.
The Valfierno accomplice story (Karl Decker, 1932) and the suggestion that an associate who made copies motivated Peruggia are left out as unconfirmed.
